blocks.text: Root → Left → Right. The first DFS pattern visit the node before exploring its subtrees.
Preorder traversal is a depth-first traversal where you visit the current node first, then recursively traverse the left subtree, then the right subtree.
The word "pre" means the root is processed before (pre) its children. This is in contrast to inorder (root in the middle) and postorder (root last).
Think of it like reading a book's table of contents: you see the chapter title first, then go into the sections inside it. Root = chapter, subtrees = sections.
Here's the tree we'll trace. Watch the order: always process the node the moment you arrive at it, before going left or right

items: Step 1: Visit Node 1: Preorder starts with the root node, so we visit 1 first and add it to the result. After processing the root, we move to its left child. Result: 1
Step 2: Visit Node 2: We arrive at node 2 and process it immediately. Since preorder visits the left subtree first, we continue to node 4. Result: 1 → 2
Step 3: Visit Node 4: Node 4 is visited and added to the result. Since it has no children, we return back to node 2. Result:1 → 2 → 4
Step 4: Visit Node 5: The left subtree of node 2 is complete, so we now visit its right child 5. Since 5 is also a leaf node, we return to the root. Result: 1 → 2 → 4 → 5
Step 5: Visit Node 3: The entire left subtree of the root has been processed, so we move to the right child 3. After visiting 3, we continue to its left child. Result: 1 → 2 → 4 → 5 → 3
Step 6: Visit Node 6: Node 6 is visited and added to the result. Since it has no children, we return back to node 3. Result: 1 → 2 → 4 → 5 → 3 → 6
Step 7: Visit Node 7: The left subtree of 3 is complete, so we visit its right child 7. This is the final node in the traversal. Result: 1 → 2 → 4 → 5 → 3 → 6 → 7

blocks.text: Final Traversal: 1 → 2 → 4 → 5 → 3 → 6 → 7. The key idea is that preorder always follows Root → Left → Right, completely finishing the left subtree before moving to the right subtree.
The recursive version is 3 lines of logic. The base case handles null nodes. Everything else follows from the Root → Left → Right order.
For iterative preorder, we use a stack. The key insight: push right child before left child, because the stack is LIFO so left gets popped (processed) first.
Remember: push right before left. Stack is LIFO, so left gets popped first. This is the #1 mistake in iterative preorder.
Time Complexity: Preorder traversal has a time complexity of O(n) because every node in the tree is visited exactly once. No node is skipped, and no node is processed more than once.

Space Complexity: Preorder traversal has a space complexity of O(h), where h is the height of the tree. This space is used by the recursion stack. For a balanced tree, the height is O(log n), while for a completely skewed tree, the height becomes O(n), resulting in the worst-case space complexity of O(n).

items: Copying/cloning a tree: you need the root before you can attach children.
Serializing a tree: preorder gives enough info to reconstruct the structure.
Printing directory structure: folder name before its contents.
Prefix expression trees: operators come before operands (prefix notation).
Path problems: track the path from root to current node as you go down.

codes.javascript:
void preorder(node)  { visit(node); go(left); go(right); } // Root first

void inorder(node)   { go(left); visit(node); go(right); } // Root middle

void postorder(node) { go(left); go(right); visit(node); } // Root last

blocks.text: The only difference between all three DFS traversals is when you process the node relative to the recursive calls. One line moves, everything changes.

items: In iterative version: pushing left before right: this reverses the order.
Forgetting the null/base case: causes null pointer errors.
Confusing preorder with level order: preorder is DFS (stack/recursion), level order is BFS (queue).
In path problems: not backtracking: if you add to a path list, remove it on the way back up.
Assuming preorder output uniquely identifies a tree: it doesn't without inorder or null markers.
